First SST project wins to the data center: At the 2025 CDCC Summit on November 
24, Delta  announced its first solid-state transformer (SST) project for data centers 
together with Meituan and Chindata  in China. The SST features 98.5% conversion 
efficiency with output power up to 1MW for an area size of one square meter, >50% 
space saving. It could design for 240V/400V/800V DC power architecture and 
smart adjustment for GPU load volatility.  
Fuel cell production kicks off in 2H26: Delta has been working on the 
development of these for >20 years. It licensed from Ceres Power in the UK for 
both SOFC and SOEC technology in January 2024. The production will be located in 
Taiwan initially with pilot run starting from 2H26. This is part of its cohesive power 
solution offerings for DC (direct current) power architecture, in addition to smart 
micro grid management and energy storage system. That helps to off-load the 
burden from Tower to distributed power grid for data centers.  
Modular power solution offering  with Siemens: On November 19, Delta Thailand, 
Delta's 64%-owned subsidiary, announced it will partner with Siemens Smart 
Infrastructure to deliver prefabricated modular power solutions.  This aims to reduce 
time-to-market by up to 50% with plug-and-play approach, up to 20% capex 
spending and up to 27% carbon emissions. Siemens will handle electrical power 
distribution and engineering services while Delta provides high-efficiency UPS, 
battery and cooling equipment.

decline on seasonality; meanwhile, we are seeing more signs of sustainable

should  continue to see share gains with undemanding  valuation of 20x
2026e P/E  (vs. average of 25x since 2020). The combination of lukewarm
growth and hefty valuation (29x 2026e P/E now vs. average of 26x since
2020) leads to unattractive risk-reward for Hiwin.

 AirTAC International (1590.TW)  
Base case, 25x 2026e P/E. We believe this methodology better captures earnings growth 
momentum for industrial automation component plays (market sentiment moves along with 
business cycles). With a moderate recovery scenario playing out, we think the mid-cycle 
average of 25x P/E should be reasonable, though further re-rating to the peak cycle valuation 
of 30x P/E or higher would take a stronger growth outlook.
 Risks to Upside  
n Stronger macroeconomic climate in China
n Stronger-than-expected demand from industrial automation
 Risks to Downside  
n Sharper economic downturn in China
n Miniature linear guideway business development taking more time
n Larger-than-expected investment in new products but weaker-than-expected demand
 Hiwin Technologies Corp. (2049.TW)  
Base case, P/E. We think this valuation methodology better captures earnings growth 
momentum for Hiwin, because its valuation tends to move along with the business cycle. We 
apply a target multiple of 24x to our 2026 EPS estimate; we view this multiple as justified by 
the operating profit CAGR that we see of 20% for 2024-27. 
 Risks to Upside  
n Stronger industrial automation demand pickup
n Market share gains
n Earlier than expected revenue contribution from humanoids
 Risks to Downside  
n Weaker industrial automation demand
n More pricing pressure
n Market share loss 
n More broad-based impact on the global economy from geopolitical risks

Not the time to take profits: Starting from late 2Q, we had expected that  old 
memory undersupply would drive a super-cycle (link). We also built our own DDR4, 
SLC, MLC, and NOR Flash model (link). Old memory contract pricing started to pick 
up in late 3Q. A pure old memory up-cycle usually lasts for 3-4 quarters, which 
suggests that it's not the time to take profit now. Consensus earnings could increase 
very meaningfully in 2026.
Could there be more DDR4 upside? Yes: The preliminary pricing negotiations for 
1Q26 look even more favorable for  suppliers. The major reason is the demand 
coming from enterprises (link), which could push  contract pricing up >100% in 1Q26. 
Meanwhile,  DDR4 16Gb is in the most significant shortage. We believe inventory in 
channels is close to zero, with spot pricing as high as US$100, compared to spot 
price of US$45.5 according to DRAMeXchange.
The supply cut is driving up all the Flash products: The supply cut in MLC NAND is 
a big issue (link), and now we also expect some  NOR cuts as well. Given the low 
wafer value and back-end pricing hike, we believe some NOR suppliers could 
reallocate their NOR capacity to  other products. We thus expect  NOR undersupply 
in 2026 could widen to high single digits from low to mid single digits. NOR pricing 
could go up >20% in 1Q26. 
Reiterate bullish view on old memory stocks; Top Pick remains Winbond: The 
market is concerned about the pricing upside in 2026 and the disruption to 
downstream customers. Memory is always cyclical, but it's rare to see an up-cycle 
last for just one quarter. Our Top Pick remains Winbond –  there could be more 
upside to both NOR and DRAM pricing as well as bit shipment output into 2026. 
The current valuation is 2.0x 2026e BVPS, vs. ongoing ROE expansion potentially to 
30% in 2027. We also like Nanya Tech, which  reported November sales of  +29% M/

Wiwynn Corp  | Asia Pacific
Potentially positive 
developments for ASIC server 
business 
Our supply chain checks  indicate potentially  positive developments for Wiwynn's 
ASIC server business. Currently it is a major supplier for Amazon's ASIC server racks, 
but our checks indicate that Wiwynn may have seen positive developments in 
collaborating with Amazon (covered by Brian Nowak)  in board-level assembly, UBB 
(universal baseboard) or L6 assembly, with  production potentially in Malaysia and/
or Taiwan. Neither company has commented.
Potential implications for Wiwynn: The board-level business carries low ASP but 
high margin, so while any such development would not have a meaningful impact on 
the top line, it could be beneficial to margins. We recently downgraded Wiwynn to 
EW (report here), because  we believed ASIC server rack shipments would peak in 
3Q and enter a transition period in 4Q25-2Q26 before the next generation ramps in 
2H26. If Wiwynn is able to enter  the UBB business with Amazon, this could be a 
positive for Wiwynn stock.

本業獲利漸入佳境，營業利益已連續五個季度創下新高，隨新產能開

2. 
最大客戶網通機櫃訂單除由美國擴展至歐亞，產品更延伸至AI 機櫃，

率升值幅度有限，雖礙於產能滿載，營收估小幅季增2%，然預期營益率將有

Switch Rack 維持高雙位數成長，AI 伺服器隨產能開出將翻倍成長   
大型CSP 資料中心通常約配置1,500~2,000 個伺服器機櫃，雖伺服器機櫃中配置交換器於機櫃頂端，然大型資料
中心通常會在額外於資料中心設置網通機櫃以利管理網路，過往在通用伺服器為主體的資料中心，伺服器機櫃搭配
網通機櫃的相對配比較低，推估僅約低至中個位數水準，估一個資料中心若有千個伺服器機櫃，僅需配置數十個網
通機櫃即可因應高速網路傳輸。然在AI 浪潮崛起後，AI 伺服器資料中心呈現高密度的配置，預期高階AI 伺服器搭
配網通機櫃的比重將拉升數倍，以反映AI 伺服器更高密度的網路需求。 
 
以神雲大客戶資本支出需求觀察，美系CSP 2025 財年資本支出213 億美元，YoY+209%，市場共識26~27 財年

AI 伺服器產品，未來將維持高速成長。神達另有數個Tier 2 CSP 客戶，如資安業者等，雖營運規模較低，主要出貨

資料中心市場規模持續看增 
隨著數據需求增長和新興技術發展，資料中心市場規模持續擴大。企業和組織需要資料
中心的基礎設施和技術來處理大量數據，支援數位轉型和創新。AI、物聯網和大數據等
技術的推動，以及雲計算的普及，進一步推動了資料中心市場的成長。根據Prescient & 
Strategic研究數據所示，資料中心市場規模預計將從2021年的2,200億美金成長至2030
年的3,436億美金，年複合成長率為5.1%，市場規模成長除了數據量急劇增長外，主係
因政府單位積極推廣數位經濟及建置網路基礎設施，其中超過40%的市場成長動能將來
自於北美地區。

AMAX 旗下美國營運主體係於1984 年設立於加州矽谷，成立迄今已將近40 年，經此長
年累月的耕耘與發展，已獲得多家國際知名企業之青睞，擁有相對穩定的業績來源；再

2. 專業團隊打造全面性的客製化服務 
AMAX 為專業的客製化解決方案及相關伺服器、集群、整機櫃及工作站(Work Station)
製造業者，非專注於單一電子零組件產銷之廠商，故具備完整之統整能力，熟知各項硬
體、電路及散熱設備搭配之優缺點，配合客戶積極朝向雲端化、智慧化及環保減碳的目
標發展，能以專案方式給予客戶全面的IT 架構建置服務與解決方案，其專業團隊在生
產技術、研發能力、行銷通路建構上，均已有豐富之經驗。 
3. 既有客戶多元，產品應用領域廣泛

存、分析及應用等功能，使大數據系統得以從龐大混雜的數據中挖掘出有價值的資訊，

而，無論是傳統資料處理技術或大數據科技，皆具有應用領域廣泛之特色，舉凡教育、
交通、醫療、運動、網購等，均有資料處理需求，而該產業近年來正處於傳統資料處理
轉移至大數據科技時代的過渡期，故其業務發展機會甚為多元。以AMAX而言，現已有
電腦防毒軟體、人工智能、通訊、自動駕駛、半導體、石化等客戶，在既有客戶多元且
產品應用領域廣泛的利基下，AMAX擁有對外的競爭基礎及未來業務拓展的機會。

目前國內大型上市企業如台積電(2330)、聯電(2303)與日月光(3711)之2030
年中期目標分年達到RE60、RE50 與RE42，預期綠電需求逾200 億度，為

EPS 9.8 元。 
 
國內外業務雙管齊下，2026 年維持高速增長，EPS 13 元 
展望2026 年，在台灣方面預期在太陽能案場/儲能案場目標再開發各
200MW；在海外佈局方面，泓德能源積極往日本、澳洲與菲律賓發展，目前
拓展進度已超越台灣，預期澳洲Solar River 光儲案場合計約500MW 將逐步
開始認列，菲律賓方面開發1GW 太陽能案場，其中第一階段300MW 將開

引進三菱電機注資且成立合資公司，將聯手推動再生能源聚合及電網儲能業
務。綜上所述，兆豐國際認為雖短期國內市場遭遇逆風，不過泓德能源積極

APAC Focus: The coolest theme in AI  – direct 
liquid cooling for AI acceleratorsPlease refer to the narrative of this report for an explanation of this image/chart
We believe the market does not yet fully appreciate the scale and speed of the 
upcoming AI server rack liquid-cooling cycle, particularly for direct liquid cooling 
(DLC),  a technology that applies precise liquid cooling to the heat-generating 
component. We think the potential market growth outweighs pricing pressure, 
component commoditisation and ODM competition risks. Our differentiated 
bottom-up DLC TAM analysis suggests a DLC market CAGR of 51%  over 2025-30E, 
reaching US$31bn. In addition to Delta, we initiate coverage of three stocks with 
exposure to this space – AVC, Auras and top pick Jentech – all rated Buy. 
The AI thermal wall: liquid cooling is the new standard 
As genAI scales, silicon power density exceeding 1,000W TDP is driving the adoption of 
liquid-enabled thermal management. Direct-to-chip liquid cooling (DLC) is now a critical 
infrastructure requirement for leading-edge AI racks in the Nvidia Grace Blackwell/Vera 
Rubin era and beyond. See the thermal technologies 101: I. From watts to kilowatts . 
A bifurcated direct liquid cooling roadmap: micro channel lid and cold plate 
We see a market divided in two by power density. Micro-channel lids (MCL)  – integrated 
directly into the heatspreader with the lid atop the silicon –  are set to serve applications 
above 3,500W TDP. We believe adoption of MCL could start minimally in Q426E with 
overclocked NVIDIA VR200 (2,300W) and potentially become the standard for VR300 
(3,600W). We estimate TAM for MCL at US$35m/US$1.25bn in 2026E/27E, reaching US
$2.7bn in 2030E. 
Cold plate to remain mainstream; pricing concerns overdone
Cold plates should remain dominant for applications under 3,500W. We see the 
upgraded micro-channel cold plates (MCCP) being adopted for baseline Nvidia VR200 
(1,800W TDP) and ex-Nvidia GPUs and AI ASICs. We think cold plate pricing concerns 
are overdone, being outweighed by content value attachment increase per rack and DLC 
TAM expansion as AI ASIC migration to cold plate liquid cooling rises. We model cold 
plate TAM reaching US$4.4bn in 2027E and US$8.9bn in 2030E, even with our forecast 
of  50% compression in the cold plate ASP  due to potential standardisation. 
Initiate on AVC, Auras and Jentech with Buy ratings; Delta also a beneficiary
We initiate coverage of cold plate leader AVC (NT$2,000 price target), MCL leader 
Jentech (NT$5,000 price target), and Auras (NT$1,380 price target), which has a 
strengthening position in the DLC market, with Buy ratings. We also view Delta as a 
beneficiary through its strong market position in L2A sidecars.

Q: Is the data centre direct-liquid cooling (DLC) market set for growth and expansion 
despite component  pricing concerns?
Yes. Our differentiated  DLC TAM analysis indicates a data centre DLC market CAGR of 51% over 
2025-30E, from US$1.14bn in 2024 to US$31bn in 2030E despite our forecast of cold plate 
(compute tray) pricing falling around 50%, starting with VR200, amid recent Nvidia pricing concerns 
due to design standardisation and procurement consolidation. The rapid expansion of the market 
should more than offset pricing erosion, given AI ASIC and AMD could ramp up with higher value-
adds for DLC vendors, Nvidia systems have aggressive TDP roadmaps, and server CPUs could follow 
suit. In view of increasing water scarcity, we think demand for liquid cooling extends beyond AI.
Q: Could immersion cooling emerge and overtake DLC as the go-to liquid cooling method?
Unlikely. We see DLC being preferred over immersion due to its superior Total Cost of Ownership 
(TCO), retrofit viability, operational simplicity and cost efficiency. Immersion cooling faces adoption 
barriers, including architectural overhaul, hardware compatibility issues and high fluid costs. 
Q: Is micro channel lid (MCL) poised to be adopted for future leading-edge AI server rack 
solution? If so, can it supplant cold plate in DLC as the go-to method? 
We think MLC adoption is likely, but cold plate remains the mainstream DLC solution. Adoption of 
MCL is likely to start small with overclocked VR200 SKU (~2,300W TDP) by Q426E, and expect 
mainstream use to begin with NVL576 platforms in H227E for VR300  (3,600W TDP) for more 
efficient heat dissipation and future-proofing for Feynman (F200) in H228.  We expect F200 TDP to 
reach 5,000 - 7,000W. Cold plates should remain the dominant DLC solution for below 3,500W TDP 
applications with a  US$8.9bn TAM by 2030E, and a  MCL TAM of US$2.7bn by 2030E. 
We view the market as pricing in a commodisation  case for cold plates and a delay in MCL, and 
believe the market's current valuations fail to capture the potential structural DLC supercycle growth. 
AVC is trading at 20x NTM consensus PE (below  its 22x average), while Auras is trading at 18x NTM 
consensus PE (below its  20x average) and Jentech is trading at 52x NTM consensus PE, which we 
believe is due to consensus substantially underestimating Jentech's 2026E/27E EPS (8%/28% below 
our EPS estimates). 
We initiate coverage of AVC, Auras and Jentech, all with Buy ratings, as: 1) DLC market TAM 
expansion and cold plate/MCL volume and content should grow driven by rising penetration; 2) AVC 
should sustain its leading cold plate market position with leading-edge AI GPU/ASIC projects; 3) 
Auras is strengthening its liquid cooling offerings to capture the liquid cooling supercycle; and 4) 
Jentech is set to grow exponentially through the adoption of MCL potentially starting minimally in 
Q426E and ramping up to mass adoption by H227E.  
Our conviction is grounded in our proprietary top-down and bottom-up DLC TAM analysis. We 
estimate at above 2,300W, standard TIM 2 layers cause an unmanageable 20 degrees Celsius spike, 
potentially triggering early pull-in for next-gen liquid cooling, namely MCL. Our bottom-up model 
shows DLC content per rack quadrupling from US$74K (GB200 NVL72) in 2025 to US$397K by

Technical Primer: the battle against thermal resistance
The thermal interface material problem: A standard AI chip is packaged like a 
sandwich. To cool it, heat must travel from the silicon to the thermal interface material 
(TIM 1) to the heat spreader (lid), then to TIM 2, and finally to the cold plate. The critical 
thermal bottleneck is TIM 2. Since TIM 1 is die-to-lid, it is extremely thin (~30μm, high-
performance thermal conductivity material, such as graphene), and is not a thermal 
bottleneck. TIM 2 is lid-to-cold plate and is considered the thermal bottleneck for future 
AI XPUs as TIM 2 is thick (~100-150μm).

Why is TIM 2 so thick? As XPU packages get larger, they are not perfectly flat and 
they warp slightly. A standard cold plate is bulky and it is too stiff to conform to the 
microscopic warpage of the chip lid. Therefore, to prevent air gaps, vendors must 
use a thick layer of TIM 2 to act as a gap filler. 

The consequence: With the amount of thermal resistance building up from the 
silicon, before the water even starts cooling, the chip is already around 20 degrees 
Celsius hotter just trying to push heat through TIM 2. 

The solution: We view TIM 2 as a major thermal bottleneck for future AI 
platforms and believe micro-channel lid (MCL) is the solution. MCL integrates the 
water channels inside the lid and eliminates the need for TIM 2 completely. The 
thermal resistance of that layer drops to zero.

1. The acceleration thesis: Competition driving potential MCL pull-in
The consensus view: MCL are too complex, yields are too low, and cold plates are
adequate for now. Meaningful MCL adoption will not happen until late 2027/2028.
Our contrarian view: Nvidia does not have the luxury of time. The rise of AMD's MI-
series and the rapid efficiency gains of Google TPU threaten Nvidia's total cost of
ownership (TCO) dominance. To stay ahead, Nvidia could push TDP to 2,300W-plus
sooner than expected, potentially accelerating the thermal roadmap.
The catalyst: The Q426E overclocked  Nvidia VR200 SKU: We believe MCL adoption
could start small in Q426E via a specialized, overclocked SKU of the Nvidia VR200 that
raises TDP to 2,300W vs 1,800 for the standard SKU .

This SKU allows Nvidia to debug the complex MCL supply chain on a lower-
volume, high-margin product and this effectively de-risks the technology for the 
potential mass launch of the VR300 (Kyber) platform (3,600W TDP) and the future 
Feynman (F200) platform (5,000W to 7,000W). By the time 3,600W becomes 
standard, the MCL supply chain could be relatively mature. 
2. Market bifurcation: Why cold plates are unlikely  to be commoditised
The consensus view: As MCL takes over the high end, the traditional cold plate market
will suffer from volume cannibalisation and pricing pressure due to commoditisation.
Our contrarian view: In our view, the market is not shrinking, it is bifurcating. We think
the 'death' of cold plate has been vastly exaggerated, because the entire floor of the
market is rising.

While we expect the below 3,500W TDP AI GPUs to migrate to MCL, we foresee 
the large mainstream layer – including the standard VR200 (1,800W), AMD 
accelerators and the booming AI ASIC market – becoming standardised with 
upgraded micro-channel cold plates (MCCP) where  suppliers are shifting from 
150-micron to 80-100 micron channels to handle rising heat flux.

Making waves - Direct liquid cooling on the rise 
Direct liquid cooling (DLC) should remain the main liquid cooling method.   In our 
view, direct liquid cooling (DLC)  – a targeted liquid cooling approach that pumps liquid 
coolant directly through cold plates/MCL that are in physical contact with heat-
generating XPUs, specifically in  cold plate and MCL based systems –  will be the 
dominant architecture throughout the forecast period. DLC offers a pragmatic and 
economically viable pathway for both new greenfield data centres and critically the 
retrofitting of the vast installed base of brownfield facilities. Its superior thermal 
properties, proven scalability, and lower initial capex relative to alternatives make it the 
go-to solution. Immersion cooling, while theoretically potent, faces significant near-term 
barriers, including a lack of certification from key players, like Nvidia, prohibitive 
retrofitting costs, and significant operational complexity. We do not anticipate 
meaningful adoption of immersion cooling until after 2030.

Further supporting our thesis, we note leading power IC/module vendors (Infineon, 
MPS, Vicor, Delta, Flex) signal future  leading-edge AI racks approaching above 1MW and

DLC to be the go-to liquid cooling option over other liquid cooling methods, 
such as immersion cooling.While DLC and immersion cooling both offer superior 
thermal performance over air, we believe through comparative analysis of their 
deployment economics, operational practicality, and TCO reveals that DLC is positioned 
to remain the mainstream solution, making its component ecosystem an attractive 
target through TAM expansion. 
Immersion cooling is overkill with significant barriers to adoption. As outlined in 
the section above, immersion cooling captures 100% of the heat generated and can 
support extreme compute densities, but for the vast majority of current and mid-term 
future AI server rack applications, it is an 'overkill' solution and presents significant 
barriers to adoption. In our view, DLC has clearly become the most rational solution to 
adopt, even more so when analysing TCO and retrofit viability. 

Deployment and Infrastructure costs: Immersion cooling requires a complete 
architectural overhaul. It necessitates specialised 'bathtubs' and complex 
plumbing for the expensive dielectric fluids, and requires structural reinforcement 
of the data centre floor to support the immense weight of the fluid-filled tanks. 
DLC, on the other hand, can be retrofitted into existing air-cooled data centres 
with far more manageable modifications. The core components fit within server 
chassis and racks, allowing for an incremental, rack-by-rack adoption strategy. 

Hardware compatibility and warranty: Immersion cooling requires heavily 
modified or purpose-built servers, as standard IT hardware is not designed for 
submersion. This can void manufacturer warranties, a significant risk for 
operators, and creates vendor lock-in. 

Maintenance and operations: Servicing an immersion-cooled server is a 
complex and messy process, requiring the hardware to be lifted from the tank and 
cleaned of the oily dielectric fluid before any work can be done. DLC systems are 
far simpler to service; the flow of coolant can be stopped, and non-spill quick 
disconnects (QDs) allow for the clean and easy removal of a server from the rack, 
mirroring the familiar workflow of air-cooled systems. 

Energy and fluid costs: While both methods save energy compared with air 
cooling, DLC has a distinct advantage in fluid dynamics. Water, or a water-glycol 
mixture, the standard coolant for DLC, has a 4.5x higher thermal conductivity and 
a heat capacity twice that of the dielectric oils used in immersion. Water is also far 
less viscous, meaning less energy is required to pump it through the system. 
Furthermore, the dielectric fluids themselves are significantly more expensive than 
treated water.  

Unlikely to get qualified by developers:  With the challenges outlined above, 
we believe it is unlikely that full-stack (chip to rack) developers would qualify the 
immersion cooling solutions in the foreseeable future. As the ultimate driver of the 
technology, it is crucial that it is qualified before any meaningful adoption or 
testing. With thermal limits seemingly increasing for DLC through innovation such 
as micro-channels, we think it is fair to assume DLC would continue to be the go-
to technology and account for at least 95% of all liquid cooling applications for 
HPC in the coming years.

Asia Hardware Insights 5 December 2025

Core thermal technologies/methodologies 101
The fundamental catalyst for the transition from air to liquid cooling in data centres has 
been driven by  the thermal output of AI hardware, which is  exceeding the physical limits 
of air. The transition from traditional CPUs to power-hungry GPUs and custom AI 
accelerators or application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) has created a thermal 
challenge at the component, server and rack levels, making the adoption of liquid 
cooling not a choice, but a necessity. 
The entire field of data centre cooling is built upon the first law of thermodynamics in 
physics. Within a data centre, almost 100% of the electrical energy consumed by 
servers, storage arrays, networking gears, and power distribution/supply equipment is 
converted into thermal energy or heat. For example, a data centre consuming 1MW of 
electricity under its IT load will concurrently produce 1MW of heat that must be 
continuously and reliably removed. 
I. From watts to kilowatts
The evolution of air cooling: from primary cooling to heat rejection. For decades, 
data centre cooling has been dominated by air-based systems, primarily Computer 
Room Air Conditioners (CRACs) and Computer Room Air Handlers (CRAHs). These 
systems have been pushed to their physical limits by leading-edge AI computing. The 
physical properties of air fundamentally limit its ability to efficiently absorb and transport 
the immense heat generated by AI infrastructure. 
That said, we do not see air cooling disappearing, but rather evolving. We foresee a shift 
toward Air-Assisted Liquid Cooling (AALC) technologies, such as Rear Door Heat 
Exchangers (RDHx) (See Figure 34Rear-Dor Heat Exchanger (RDHx) diagram

To manage and improve data centre operations, the industry relies on a set of 
KPIs to measure efficiency. 
Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE). The PUE metric would measure how efficiently a 
data centre uses energy, comparing the total energy consumed by the entire facility to 
the energy delivered directly to the IT equipment. An ideal PUE is 1.0, which would imply 
a perfectly efficient data centre where 100% of the energy is consumed by the IT 
equipment, with no energy spent on cooling or other overheads. The industry average 
PUE has fallen from a highly inefficient 2.5 in 2007 to approx. 1.57 in 2021 and trending 
even lower in these recent years. Today, new data centres utilising modern cooling 
technologies (especially liquid  cooling) have resulted in a lower PUE of around 1.2 to 1.4 
with leading hyperscalers like Google and AWS reporting PUE of 1.1 to 1.15. 
However, PUE does not account for variations in climate, the efficiency of the IT 
equipment itself, or the potential for energy reuse (e.g., waste heat recovery). PUE can 
also be a misleading indicator when evaluating the benefits of liquid cooling. A primary 
advantage of DLC is the ability to remove server fans, which are considered part of the 
"IT Equipment Energy" in the PUE denominator. Removing these fans reduces the 
denominator's value. Even though the overall "Total Facility Energy" (the numerator) 
also decreases due to a more efficient cooling system, the resulting ratio may not 
improve as dramatically as the actual energy savings would suggest. 
To provide a clearer picture of the data centre sustainability and efficiency, the 
industry is adopting additional metrics. 
Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE): This metric measures the data centre's water 
consumption relative to the energy consumed by its IT equipment. It is calculated as the 
total site water usage (litres) /IT equipment energy (kW). A lower WUE value indicates 
greater water efficiency, with a goal of approaching zero. 
Further, in view of considerations around increasing water scarcity and drought (both 
political and operational), we anticipate that the applicability of liquid cooling extends 
beyond AI-related offerings. UBS Evidence Lab data shows that ~50% of assets of 
traditional DCs are located in areas of high or extreme water stress, and as such liquid 
cooling could become increasingly attractive to mitigate operational issues linked to 
water shortages, including permissions or approvals.

Total Usage Effectiveness (TUE): Proposed as a more accurate successor to PUE for 
liquid-cooled environments, TUE refines the denominator to focus only on the core 
processing components, thereby removing the ambiguity caused by auxiliary 
components such as server fans. The formula is Total Facility Energy/Energy Consumed 
by Core IT functions. 
Beyond facility-level efficiency metrics, a set of more granular engineering metrics is 
used to design and evaluate the performance of specific cooling components and 
systems. 
Thermal Resistance: One of the most important metric for a cooling component like a 
cold plate, measured in Celsius per watt (C/W) or Kelvins per watt (K/W). It quantifies the 
temperature increase of a component for every watt of heat it generates. A lower 
thermal resistance indicates better cooling performance. For example, microchannel 
cold plates (MCCP) can achieve a thermal resistance of 0.07 K/W. 
The primary catalyst to shift from air to liquid cooling is the exponential 
increase in the heat generated by modern processors/accelerators.Traditional air 
cooling, even when optimised with containment and economisation, is generally 
effective for server racks with power densities up to ~20-0kW. In highly engineered air-
cooled environments, this limit can be pushed to perhaps 30-40kW per rack, but this is 
widely considered the ceiling for practical air cooling. With leading-edge AI server racks 
reaching 120kW (GB200 NVL72), 140kW (GB300 NVL72), 250-380kW (VR200 
NVL144), and above 600kW to potentially 1MW (VR300 NVL576), the sheer volume of 
air required to remove the heat becomes impractical, and the power consumed by the 
fans needed to move that air becomes a significant portion of the total energy budget, 
leading to diminishing returns in cooling efficiency. 
Liquids are superior to air in their ability to absorb and transport heat, as they 
have over 3,500x the heat capacity of air by volume. A much smaller volume of 
water can absorb and transport the same amount of heat as large volume of air.
Rear-Door Heat Exchangers (RDHx). A RDHx is a prime example of a hybrid air-liquid 
solution. It replaces the standard rear door of a server rack with a large, liquid-cooled 
radiator. The fundamental principle is to intercept and neutralise the heat from the 
server exhaust air at the rack level, before it can escape into the data hall. The hot air 
exhausted or expelled  from the back of the server is forced to pass through the heat 
exchanger coils of the RDHx. A liquid coolant, typically chilled water from the facility's 
central plant, circulates through these coils, absorbing the heat from the air. The now-
cooled air is then discharged into the hot aisle at or near the ambient room temperature.

exchanger coils with no additional power draws. Their simplicity makes them 
highly reliable, energy-efficient, and low-maintenance. They are best suited for 
moderate heat loads. 

Active RDHx. These units integrate a wall of its own fans into the door rack door 
assembly. These fans actively pull the hot air from the servers and through the heat 
exchanger, providing more consistent airflow and enabling the system to handle 
much higher thermal densities - up to 100kW per rack in some models. 
In-Row Heat Exchangers (IRHX). Introduced by AWS in July 2025 when it introduced 
the concept of scalable heat exchanger side cars after rejecting off-the-shelf (OTC) 
solutions, thinking current DLC solutions would take up too much data centre floor 
space or increase water usage. An IRHX is an air-liquid cooling system that can be fit 
between server racks in the same row, rather than being attached to the rear door. AWS 
has been deploying IRHX systems across its newer high-density data halls to handle the 
localised thermal output of its Nvidia GB200 NVL72 clusters. The design captures hot 
exhaust air immediately as it exits the servers, routing it through liquid-cooled coils 
within the IRHX before it re-enters the cold aisle. The coolant is circulated to a Coolant 
Distribution Unit (CDU) or facility loop, where heat is rejected via dry coolers or chillers.
Direct-Liquid-Cooling (DLC).DLC is one of the most pragmatic and widely adopted 
forms of liquid cooling today, and we believe this liquid cooling methodology will remain 
the go-to and mainstream option for liquid cooling throughout our forecast period to 
2030. Rather than attempting to cool an entire server, rack, or room with a layer of cold 
fluid, DLC takes a targeted approach by applying cooling precisely where it is needed the 
most. It places heat-dissipating materials (cold plates) directly on the surfaces of heat-
generating components (GPU/CPU/NIC/Switch, etc). This method's ability to integrate 
into existing data centres makes it a crucial transitional technology, bridging the gap 
between the air-cooled past and the liquid-cooled future.
Single-Phase vs. Two-Phase DLC. The core principle of DLC is to capture of majority of 
a server's heat at its source (CPUs/CPUs/NICs/Switches). This is achieved by placing a 
liquid-filled heat exchanger, known as a cold plate, directly onto the chip. There are two 
primary methods of DLC. 

Single-Phase DLC:This is the most common and straightforward implementation. 
A liquid coolant, typically a mixture of water and glycol (to prevent corrosion and 
biological growth), is pumped through the cold plate. The liquid absorbs heat from 
the chip via conduction, its temperature rises, but it remains in a liquid state 
throughout the entire closed loop. The heated liquid is then circulated back to a 
coolant distribution unit (CDU) to be cooled. Its relative simplicity, lower cost, and 
reliability make it the dominant choice for current DLC setup/deployment.

Two-Phase DLC:The more advanced method that leverages the physics of phase-
change evaporation for a greater step-up of heat transfer. It uses a specialised 
dielectic fluid (fluoracarbons are often used) with a low boiling point (50c). As this 
fluid passes through the microchannels of the cold plate, the heat from the chip 
causes it to boil and turn into vapour. This process of vaporisation absorbs a large 
amount of latent heat, making it exceptionally effective at cooling. The vapour 
then travels through manifolds, tubes to a condenser (either within a CDU or 
elsewhere), where it releases its heat, condenses back into a liquid, and is 
recirculated to the cold plate. While two-phased DLC offers the highest thermal 
performance, its complexity, higher cost, and the need for specialised fluids make 
it a less common, though emerging, solution. 
The adoption of liquid cooling technologies is creating a shift in data centre design, 
operation, and skillsets required of the data centre workforce. The move from managing 
airflow to managing fluid flow introduces new complexities related to plumbing, 
hydraulics, and fluid chemistry. This is often an underestimated operational hurdle. Data 
centre teams, traditionally composed of experts in HVAC and electrical systems, must 
now develop or acquire expertise in fluid dynamics and leak mitigation. This transition, 
in our view, is one of the hidden costs of the TCO of liquid cooling and the bottleneck 
alongside data centre physical readiness before liquid cooling mass adoption.

II. Zooming in on Current DLC technologies
The fundamental principle of DLC is to move the liquid coolant as close as possible to the 
source of the heat. The system operates as a closed loop that precisely targets the 
highest power components within a server. 
The process is as follows: 

Heat absorption: A liquid coolant - typically a mixture of water and glycol for 
freeze protection, or a specialised dielectric fluid, is pumped to the server. 

Direct contact: Inside the server the coolant flows through cold plates. 

Heat transfer: Heat generated by the chip is conducted through a thermal 
interface material (TIM) into the cold plate, where it is efficiently absorbed by the 
flowing liquid. This process can capture ~70-75% of the total heat generated by 
the server directly into the liquid loop. 

Heat removal: The now-warmed liquid exits the server and is piped away to a 
coolant distribution unit to be cooled.

Thermal Interface Material (TIM). No matter how smooth the surfaces of the chip 
and the cold plate may seem, microscopic imperfections create air gaps that impede 
heat transfer. To overcome this, a layer of TIM (a thermally conductive paste or pad) is 
applied between the chips and the cold plate (See Figure 66Cold Plate DLC Solution). The TIM fills these gaps, 
ensuring an uninterrupted path for heat to conduct from the processor to the cooling 
system. Typical conductivity ranges from 3–8 W/mK for polymer greases to >50 W/mK 
for liquid TIMs. TIM 1 (the first TIM layer) is applied between the die and the IHS, and TIM 
2 (the second TIM layer) is applied between the IHS and the cold plate or heatsink, if it is 
air-cooled.

II. Immersion Cooling
Immersion Cooling. While DLC offers a precise, targeted solution, immersion cooling is 
the most comprehensive and thermally efficient approach. By completely submerging IT 
hardware in a dielectric fluid, immersion cooling eliminates the air medium entirely, 
capturing 100% of the heat generated by every component on a server/rack. This radical 
departure from traditional data centre design improves power density and energy 
efficiency, but it also introduces significant operational and implementation 
complexities. Potential issues include data centre structural floor load limitation (1 48U 
data tank could weigh up to 2,500kg when full), retrofitting (major infrastructure 
changes), maintenance and service (warranty complexity, equipment handling, 
specialised procedures, full-system downtime vs. node-maintenance for DLC), cost and 
availability (high initial costs, limited vendor support), and potential long-term chip 
performance degradation concerns. Notable vendors: Vertiv, Schneider, Asetek, 
Gigabyte, Wiwynn, Submer.

Single-Phase Immersion Cooling (1-PIC): In this method, the entire server/rack 
is submerged in a tank of dielectric oil, such as mineral oil, synthetic hydrocarbon, 
or bio-based ester. As the components generate heat, that heat is transferred 
directly to the surrounding fluid. The fluid remains in its liquid state throughout the 
process. Pumps circulate the heated fluid out of the tank to a heat exchanger, 
where the heat is transferred to a facility water loop. The now-cooled fluid is then 
returned to the tank to continue the cycle. 1-PIC systems typically use "open bath" 
tanks, which are not sealed at atmospheric pressure.

Two-Phase Immersion Cooling (2-PIC): This more complex method utilises a 
specially engineered fluorochemical fluid with a very low boiling point (50°C). The 
server/rack is also submerged in the same way vs. 1-PIC, and the heat from the 
processors causes the fluid in direct contact with them to boil, changing its state 
from liquid to vapour. This phase change, known as nucleate boiling, absorbs a 
large amount of latent heat energy, making it an efficient mode of heat transfer. 
The vapour, being less dense, rises to the top of the sealed tank, where it comes 
into contact with condenser coils (which contain cool water from the facility loop). 
The vapour transfers its heat to the coils, causing it to condense back into a liquid 
and "rain" down onto the servers below, completing a passive, closed-loop cycle 
driven by natural convection.

We note that widespread adoption of immersion cooling faces significant 
headwinds due to regulatory restrictions on PFAS fluids  (including 3M's 
planned exit), creating uncertainty around the long-term supply chain for these 
specific coolants.

III.  Micro-Channel Lid (MCL)
MCL is a shift from "on-chip" to "in-package" cooling. The current DLC setup involves 
mounting a cold plate onto the integrated heat spread (IHS) - the lid that protects the IC 
die. This creates multiple thermal interfaces: from the die to TIM 1, then to the IHS, from 
the IHS to the TIM 2, and from the TIM 2 to the cold plate. Each interface adds to the 
overall thermal resistance, impeding the flow of heat. First wave beneficiaries: 
Jentech (sole provider), Potential second-wave entrance: AVC, Auras

The MCL approach eliminates these intermediate layers. The standard IHS is replaced 
with a custom-lid that has micro-channels fabricated directly into its structure. This 
allows the coolant to flow just microns above the IC die. By removing the thermal 
resistance associated with the IHS and TIM, MCLs can achieve a level of heat extraction 
far superior to the conventional cold plates today. We think MCL could be a pragmatic 
solution for processors exceeding 3,500W per chip (package). 
The engineering process. MCL begins with a base, typically made of high-purity 
oxygen-free copper, which serves as the primary interface with the IC die below. A dense 
array of microscopic channels, with micron dimensions, is then fabricated directly into 
the top surfaces of this copper base. These channels are designed to maximise surface 
area while maintaining controlled fluid flow characteristics. A cover plate, or lid, is then 
bonded over this channelled surface to create an airtight enclosure. This lid incorporates 
precisely engineered inlet and outlet manifolds that allow coolant to be introduced, 
distributed evenly across the channel array, and then collected after absorbing heat. The 
engineering and creation of the channels may involve processes like advanced skived 
fins, high-precision CNC, vacuum brazing, electroplating, and could potentially utilise 
chemical etching, micro-milling, laser cutting, or ECAM (3D printing), to achieved the 
required precision and surface/interior finish. The sealing of the lid is also crucial, as it 
must be accomplished without any contaminants or creating thermal stresses that could 
compromise the package's integrity. Advanced bonding techniques such as diffusion 
bonding or fluxless brazing under a controlled atmosphere are required to create a 
permanent, leak-proof seal that can withstand the pressure and thermal cycling of the 
operational environment. This entire process must also be conducted with extreme 
cleanliness to prevent any particulate matter from entering and obstructing the micro 
channels.
III. Performance Metrics/Challenges for DLC
The effectiveness of a DLC system is measured by several key metrics, which also 
highlight its inherent trade-offs. 

Heat Flux: This quantifies the rate of heat transfer per unit of area, measuring the 
intensity of heat generated in a concentrated space. It is expressed in watts per 
square cm (W/cm^2). As processors become more powerful and compact, their 
heat flux increases significantly, which is a primary reason traditional air cooling is 
no longer sufficient. Advanced cooling solutions are evaluated by their ability to 
handle high heat flux, with some micro-channel systems designed to manage 
loads of 200 W/cm^2 or more. 

Thermal Resistance:  Measured in C/W or K/, this is the most important metric. It 
quantifies the temperature increase of the component for every watt of heat it

Advanced microchannel cold plates (MCCP) can achieve thermal resistance values 
below 0.1 K/W. 

Pressure Drop: This is the measure of resistance the coolant faces as it flows 
through the cold plate's channels. High pressure drop is undesirable as it requires 
more powerful pumps, which consume more energy. The extremely small 
passages in MCLs make managing pressure drop a primary design challenge. 

Flow Rate: The volume of coolant flowing through the system, typically measured 
in liters per minute (L/min). While higher flow rates can improve cooling, they also 
increase pressure drop and pumping power, so designers aim for an optimal 
balance.

Temperature Differential: This is the change in temperature of a fluid (air or 
liquid) as it passes over a heat source or through a cooling unit. There is a fixed 
physical relationship between heat, airflow, and the temperature differential. An 
ideal cooling system would have the same temperature differential delta across the 
IT equipment as it does across the cooling units, indicating a perfectly balanced 
system. 
Limitations and Challenges 

Higher Initial Cost (capex): DLC systems carry a relatively higher upfront cost 
than air cooling systems. DLC-ready servers can be 20-30% more expensive at the 
least than their air-cooled counterparts, and the required CDU and plumbing 
infrastructure adds further expense. 

Operational Complexity: The introduction of liquid into the data hall requires 
new maintenance procedures, staff training, and monitoring protocols for fluid 
quality and potential leaks. 

Leak Risk: Although modern systems are  reliable and often use non-conductive 
dielectric fluids, the perceived risk of a coolant leak causing catastrophic damage 
to IT equipment remains a major psychological barrier to adoption for many risk-
averse operators. 

MCL Limitations: The microscopic channels in MCLs are highly susceptible to 
fouling (clogging) from even minute participles of  biological growth in the coolant, 
requiring stringent fluid filtration and maintenance. They can also suffer from flow 
instabilities and dry out in two-phase applications. Their complex fabrication also 
makes them significantly more expensive. Furthermore, the supply chain 
ecosystem and value chain would need to drastically shift if MCL were to be 
mainstream adopted as liquid cooling testing would now be conducted at the 
packaging level vs. ODM level (cold plate), which would further complicate 
packaging procedures and required equipment, with potential new vendors 
brought into the mix.
III. Potential Future Liquid Cooling Technologies
Below, we outline two potential liquid cooling technologies that are undergoing tests 
now, though we do not anticipate these methods being adopted or used meaningfully 
within our forecasted period to 2030E. 
Microfluidic Etching (Direct-to-Silicon). This advanced liquid cooling method is 
notably researched by Microsoft, and it  takes MCL to the next level by directly etching 
microscopic, vein-like channels directly into the back of the silicon die itself. This brings a 
dielectric coolant into direct contact with the silicon, eliminating TIMs and reduces 
thermal resistance significantly. 

Underlying issues: 1) The core problem is that this method integrates 
semiconductor manufacturing with plumbing, which is complex and risky. 
There is no separate cooler to attach as the micro-channels are directly etched 
onto the wafer. This adds numerous, complex MEMs-like fabrication steps to 
an already expensive chip-making process. A single flaw in an etched channel 
or a bad seal could render an entire die useless. 2) The channels are 
microscopic, making them highly susceptible to clogging from any micro-
particulates in the coolant loop over time. A clog is most likely not serviceable 
and would lead to a localised thermal failure. 3) Pumping liquid inside the chip 
package requires a perfect, long-term hermetic seal that can withstand

Jet Impingement Cooling: This is a highly intensive DLC technique where high-velocity 
jets of dielectric fluid are sprayed directly onto the surface of the die. This high-speed 
impact (impingement) disrupts the thermal boundary layer at the chip's surface, 
resulting in extremely high heat transfer coefficients. It is effective at managing the hot 
spots. Advanced forms like two-phase jet impingement further boost performance by 
leveraging vaporisation latent heat, absorbing even more amount of thermal energy in 
the process. 

Underlying issues: 1) The main issues is obvious as it uses, essentially, the 
sheer violence of the water spray to cool down the die. The "jets" must be fired 
at the die at very high velocity, which would require powerful, energy-intensive 
pumps, thus, a significant portion of the energy you save on cooling fans could 
be lost to running the high-pressure liquid pumps, defeating the purpose. 2) 
The high velocity liquid can cause erosion on the die's surface or the nozzle 
plate over time. The physical damage would degrade performance and could 
potentially cause the cooler or the chip to fail eventually. 3) The jet plate is a 
complex, custom-milled component with an array of nozzles that must align 
perfectly with the chip's known hotspots. It would be difficult to scale as the 
solution is not standardised.

Valuation Method and Risk Statement
Investing in the technology sector involves a high degree of risk. Rapid technological changes, 
increasing competition and exposure to macroeconomic cycles are among the many risks 
faced by investors in tech stocks. Moreover, it is extremely difficult to project the financial 
results of tech companies since their operating models are highly volatile and unpredictable. 
Finally, valuing tech stocks can prove challenging as neither traditional nor non-traditional 
valuation measures provide much insight into how these stocks trade.
We value AVC using PE methodology.
Key risks include: 1) slower-than-expected adoption of liquid cooling solutions in AI servers, 
which could limit core business growth; 2) intensifying price competition in the thermal 
module (cold plate) market as customers look to standardize/commoditize thermal modules; 
3) raw material cost volatility, particularly in copper and aluminum, which may impact
margins; and 4) potential fluctuation in AI/general server demand from key US hyperscaler
customers.

commoditize thermal modules; 3) volatility in raw material costs, particularly copper and

server demand; a slower-than-expected IA recovery.

關注中國需求 
 
1. 
中、長期市場需求變化仍需關注中國。中國增發國債刺激經濟增
長，顯示其救經濟的決心。若能加強基礎設施建設，將拉動長期散
裝需求。 
2. 
中國穀物進口部分由澳洲轉向南美，運程延遠，有助運費拉高。因
應減碳要求，中國大陸規劃將粗鋼產量壓減。為實現碳達峰和碳中
和，已連續進行粗鋼減產，這一目標尚未最終確定。此為潛在不利
因素。 
3. 
印度經濟發展用煤增加，吸納部分運力。 
 
 
 
產業趨勢 
 
1. 
此前中國經濟疲弱，基礎工業產能供過於求，中國增發國債刺激經
濟增長，成效不佳。現今推出人民幣1.2兆元的雅魯藏布江下游水
電工程（雅下工程），顯示其救經濟的決心。若能加強基礎設施建
設，將拉動長期散裝需求。 
2. 
其他影響運價有以下幾項：全球原物料需求持平或略增、新船訂單
佔比偏低、國際環保法規加速拆船、乾散貨延噸哩逐年成長。總體
經濟面因素則有：季節性氣候影響、美國維持高利率、大陸房市嚴
峻、運力中期恐呈過剩等因素。 
3. 
因地緣政治，中國戰略上擴大在西非投資鋁礬土礦區。預計今、明
年開採量增加回銷大陸的運輸需求，將可拉升乾散貨延噸哩增加。
此外中國大陸發展AI 需電，電力行業有近100GW燃煤電廠容量開
工建置，達近10年新高。原暫停的3.3GW工程也已復工，帶動電
煤為主的煤炭進口創歷史新高，散裝航運運煤運價有撐。 
4. 
散裝船新船交船量，扣除不符合環保必須拆除的舊船，散裝船的整
體供給可能出現低度成長。過去幾年因為造船廠塢期滿檔，貨櫃輪
排擠散裝船訂新船困難，造成今年散裝船新交船的運力低，有助於
推升散裝船舶運價。

On Dec 2nd, AirTAC reported November revenue of Rmb691mn (+10% MoM, +21% 
YoY) / NT$3,025mn (+12% MoM, +18% YoY), which was 4% higher than GSe in 
RMB.  
In November, AirTAC’s revenue was 4% higher than GSe in RMB, mainly driven by (1) 
solid CAPEX demand from the electronics industry, especially from iPhone supply 
chain (2) battery-related demand was stronger than expected in November, 
considering the ongoing import substitution trend, and (3) inventory build up 
demand from all end markets before year-end stock taking.  
On the other hand, November revenue went up 21% YoY in RMB, despite 4% YoY 
fewer working days vs. November 2024. This reflects a slowdown from the peak level 
in October (22% YoY), but is still much faster than the YT11M YoY growth of 15%. We 
believe the solid revenue YoY growth was driven by (1) solid automotive and battery 
demand, which has continued to deliver high YoY revenue growth in the past few 
quarters, (2) recovering electronics demand, thanks to better iPhone supply chain 
CAPEX outlook, (3) broad-based demand recovery as we see all segment revenues 
growing 5%+ YoY despite 4% fewer working days (vs. last November), which we 
believe is in line with the company’s commentary on improving investment 
confidence in China (see here). We see increasing confidence around investment in 
capital goods from China end customers, but we haven’t really seen any significant 
improvement in the overall non-Semi/AI/EV industries’ demand in 2026, so we will 
closely monitor the demand outlook in the coming months/quarters. 
In terms of growth by end-market segments for November, the battery sector 
continued to outgrow all other sectors (+68% YoY), followed by automotive (+25% 
YoY), machine tool (+23% YoY), packaging (+14% YoY), electronics (+13% YoY), 
textile (12% YoY), general machinery (+10% YoY) and energy lighting (+8% YoY).

We maintain our positive view on AirTAC, considering the company’s solid B/S expansion 
and FCF inflow, which should together drive the company’s ROE in coming years (ROE 
should be back to 19.1% in 2027E vs. 16-17% in 2022-24) and a high dividend payout 
ratio (50-60%+ per year) in the foreseeable future. 
Maintain Buy on AirTAC with an unchanged TP of NT$1,085. 
Investment Thesis - AirTAC 
AirTAC is the 2nd-largest pneumatic supplier in mainland China with 23% market share 
in 2023, outpacing most local competitors, owing to its low-cost yet good quality 
product, and service quality reputation in most key cities in mainland China. We forecast 
its market share will reach 28% in 2026E and expect AirTAC to be the structural winner 
in a deflationary market, due to its: (1) strong market growth and leadership: AirTAC 
continues to expand its market share in mainland China driven by competitive pricing 
that is more than 10% lower vs. international peers (with 45%+ GM / 25-30% OPM) and 
high demand elasticity among mainland China customers; and (2) superior cost structure 
and financial health: with a best-in-class cash cost and solid balance sheet, featuring 
positive net cash over FCF since 2023/24, we believe AirTAC is well-equipped to weather 
industry downturns and capitalize on market restructuring. 
Overall, we believe AirTAC will see better revenue/profitability in the long term given its 
share gainer position in the China pneumatic market and potential to gain share in the 
linear guide market (despite weak demand in the next 1-2 years). This should lead to a 
strengthened valuation, vs. its recent trading range (trading below its 10-year avg. P/E 
multiple). We are Buy rated on AirTAC. 
Price target risks and methodology - AirTAC 
Valuation methodology: Our 12m TP of NT$1,085 is based on a target P/E of 23x 
2026E avg. EPS (in-line with its mid-cycle valuation since its IPO). 
Key downside risks: (1) Stronger competition from peers; (2) sharper-than-expected 
Rmb depreciation, and (3) a longer-than-expected end-market demand downtrend in 
mainland China.

GS Factor Profile 
The Goldman Sachs Factor Profile provides investment context for a stock by comparing key attributes to the market (i.e. our universe of rated stocks)

Financial Returns and Multiple). Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple are calculated by using normalized ranks for specific metrics for each stock. The 
normalized ranks for the metrics are then averaged and converted into percentiles for the relevant attribute. The precise calculation of each metric may 
vary depending on the fiscal year, industry and region, but the standard approach is as follows: 
Growth is based on a stock’s forward-looking sales growth, EBITDA growth and EPS growth (for financial stocks, only EPS and sales growth), with a 
higher percentile indicating a higher growth company. Financial Returns is based on a stock’s forward-looking ROE, ROCE and CROCI (for financial 
stocks, only ROE), with a higher percentile indicating a company with higher financial returns. Multiple is based on a stock’s forward-looking P/E, P/B, 
price/dividend (P/D), EV/EBITDA, EV/FCF and EV/Debt Adjusted Cash Flow (DACF) (for financial stocks, only P/E, P/B and P/D), with a higher percentile 
indicating a stock trading at a higher multiple. The Integrated percentile is calculated as the average of the Growth percentile, Financial Returns 
percentile and (100% - Multiple percentile). 
Financial Returns and Multiple use the Goldman Sachs analyst forecasts at the fiscal year-end at least three quarters in the future. Growth uses inputs 
for the fiscal year at least seven quarters in the future compared with the year at least three quarters in the future (on a per-share basis for all metrics).

Expect better-than-feared 4Q25 and promising 2026 outlook
We forecast Wiwynn’s September sales to be NT$85.0bn (-11% MoM, +146% YoY) 
thanks to stronger-than-expected shipments of racks for AWS ASICs. While the 
market has been concerned about the AWS ASIC transition period starting from 
4Q25, we believe robust demand for CSP clients’ regular servers and the ramp-up
for Oracle’s GPU rack demand could mitigate this. We expect Wiwynn’s Mexico 
facility to support Oracle’s GPU rack demand, and its upcoming US plant will 
further support AWS ASIC liquid cooling rack manufacturing from 2H26. We lift 
25-27CT EPS by 6-18% and raise our TP from NT$3,600 to NT$4,200. Maintain 
Outperform.
3Q25 preview
Driven by increased cloud Capex, Wiwynn as the major AWS ASIC L10/L11 supplier
has continued to benefit from ASIC demand. With ongoing robust shipments for 
AWS Trainium2, we forecast September sales of NT$85.0bn, -11% MoM, +146% 
YoY, thanks to the robust demand for AWS ASICs, and this will lead to 3Q25CT
revenue of NT$266bn, which is 17% higher than consensus forecasts.
AWS ASIC transition impact could be mitigated
While the market has been concerned about the period of AWS’ ASIC transition 
from Trainium2 to Trainium3, we believe Wiwynn has two strong catalysts to 
mitigate any impact: regular servers and Oracle AI servers. We see continued
strength in CSP regular server demand into 4Q25. And for Oracle’s orders, 
Wiwynn’s Mexico plant could facilitate manufacturing from L10/L11. We expect 
the revenue contribution from Oracle to begin from 4Q25 and reach 5% into 2026
with upside risk.
Stronger 2026 outlook
As new US capacity comes online in end-4Q25/early-1Q26, Wiwynn will complete 
the manufacturing support for key customers’ AI server demand under the current 
uncertain US tariff conditions. Its US plant will focus on production of liquid cooling 
server racks, in line with the trend of ASIC liquid cooling adoption from 4Q25 
onwards. Into 2026, with AWS’ rising ASIC demand for Trainium3 and ongoing order
share wins in GPU racks, we forecast 2026 sales to grow 10% YoY.
Earnings revisions and valuation
We lift 25/26/27CT EPS by 6%/14%/18% to reflect the strong near-term demand 
from AWS Trainium2, higher revenue contribution from AWS Trainium3 and 
Oracle’s GPU server shipments, resulting in a higher TP of NT$4,200 (from 
NT$3,600), still based on 16x 26CT PE. Maintain Outperform.

reflects market expectations for the company’s earnings growth outlook. Our target

penetration, that could lead to a more volatile earnings profile; and 4) short supply

revenue outlook.

內容摘要 
 
受惠彩色電子紙電子書閱讀器需求強勁，今年前三季EPS 3.72元  
今年第三季營收22.96億元，季增約11%、年增約26%，為2024年第
一季以來單季新高，主要來自匯率回穩與產品組合優化。受惠彩色電
子紙電子書閱讀器需求強勁，帶動營運連續走升，惟2025上半年業外
損失較嚴重，累計今年前三季EPS 3.72元。  
 
 第四季為閱讀器傳統旺季，預期明年營收可望再雙位數成長  
展望後市，振曜看好今年第四季為閱讀器傳統旺季，加上10月營收已
創今年單月新高、6月以來逐月走揚，2025全年營收可望改寫歷史紀
錄。隨彩色閱讀器比重上升、看板業務放大以及轉投資效益持續發
酵，振曜預期2026年營收可望再雙位數成長，毛利率也可維持在目前
的高檔區間，整體成長趨勢明確。  
 
振曜看好電子看板是未來潛力新星，市場快速崛起  
 電子紙廣告看板搶進智慧交通、零售及藝術產業等三大應用主力，同
時深耕醫療應用也開始萌芽，已經出貨破千台，預估年底出貨破2,000
台，目前應用政府及大型企業為主，未來待電子看板與傳統LCD價差
從目前的五六倍降至兩至三倍的甜蜜點，可望驅動市場快速成長。

Background: We had an update with the management team on 30 
September. Founded in 1987 and listed on Taiwan’s main board in 2009, 
Jentech is a manufacturer of cooling products (74% of 1H25 revenue vs. 
66% in 2024, including heat spreader for server/AI server), lead frames 
(9% of 1H25 revenue vs. 14% in 2024), electronic components (6% of 
1H25 revenue vs. 9% in 2024), communication connectors (1% of 1H25 
revenue vs. 2% in 2024) and others (10% of 1H25 revenue vs. 10% in 
2024). The company has production sites in Taiwan and China, with a new 
plant currently under construction in Taoyuan Aerotropolis (Taiwan) mainly 
for the production of heat spreaders, cooling baseplates and server loading 
mechanisms. Jentech’s QFII holdings percentage was 28.4% as of 2 
October 2025, vs. 25.7% at the beginning of 2025. 
 
Highlights: Jentech's next-generation thermal product offerings 
include the Vapor Chamber Lid (VCL) and the Microchannel Lid (MCL). 
MCL is a chip-level cooling solution, which enables the heat removal 
required to meet the enormous thermal loads of today’s AI servers. There is 
still discussion on whether the next-generation AI platform will adopt MCL 
technology, while holding a possibility that the initial rollout may begin with 
VCL, followed by a subsequent MCL version. However, there is no final 
decision yet. 
 
Competitive edge. Jentech has a vertical integration model for its cooling 
products which incorporates elements such as design capability, mould 
processing, semiconductor level plating, machining, stamping, and injection 
moulding. Its MCL offering is designed for chip-level thermal management 
and is its highly differentiated vs. other products on the market, which sets 
a high entry barrier for its competitors. Jentech’s competitive edges: 1) Its 
equipment and process architecture are purpose-built for heat spreader 
manufacturing, reflecting a bespoke, application-driven production 
approach; 2) the firm demonstrates deep mastery of material, which 
underpins consistent product performance; 3) the operational focus on yield 
improvement directly translates into margin expansion, making process 
control a lever for profitability. Notably, the company achieves 
semiconductor-grade cleanliness not through a traditional cleanroom but 
via specialised cleaning technologies, allowing it to meet stringent quality 
requirements for its chip-level products. Jentech reported revenue of 
TWD13.3bn (+53.8% YoY) for 8M25, mainly driven by its cooling products 
for AI servers. 
 
Valuation: Per Bloomberg consensus, the stock is trading at 2025/26E 
PERs of 64.1x/41.3x, vs. its past-3-year forward trading range of 17-47x.

明年營收及獲利表現將持續向上。 
 
 
 
未來成長動能 
 
1. AI伺服器應用方面(GPU占7成；ASIC占2~3成)，公司看好明年整體
水冷散熱需求強勁，同時也看好ASIC的發展，將是公司未來成長的
一大動能。公司目前已和各大CSP客戶合作這一代及下一代ASIC專
案，同時也與NVIDIA、AMD保持密切合作，目前的ASIC仍以氣冷
方案為主，不過由於目前水冷版本仍在測試中，僅少部分的ASIC採
用水冷散熱。若後續水冷良率提升，則水冷滲透率將進一步提高。
我們預期ASIC AI伺服器未來水冷滲透率將會持續上升。 
2. 我們預估2H26 ASIC有多位客戶新世代水冷板放量，同時公司有望
切入新CSP ASIC水冷板供應。機櫃需求強勁跟降噪機櫃新產品線是
明年另一成長動能。 
3. ASIC 散熱方案由氣冷轉向液冷:目前大多數 ASIC 晶片功耗尚未超過 
1,000W，因此仍主要採用傳統氣冷方案，僅有 AWS Trainium 2.5 
和 Meta MTIA 2 等少數產品開始試行水冷散熱。然而隨著新的資料
中心逐步完成水冷基礎設施的建置，以及未來更高功率晶片的量
產，ASIC 伺服器的水冷滲透率預計將在 2026 年大幅提高。 
4. Trainium 專案詳情： 原本 Trainium 2 採用均熱板 (VC) 氣冷散熱。
從 2025 年第四季量產的 Trainium 2.5 開始，部分機型將導入水冷
散熱，且設計上分為 Compute Tray 和 Switch Tray，每個晶片都將
有獨立的水冷板，並採用 UQD (水冷轉接頭) 進行連接，其採用數量
將明顯高於 GB200/GB300 平台。 
5. 初期挑戰與未來趨勢：雖然 Trainium 3 初期水冷滲透率預計在 20% 
至 30% 之間，但長期來看，對於 Google TPU V6、Meta MTIA 2、
Microsoft Maia 2 和 AWS Trainium 3 等高功率 ASIC 而言，液冷散
熱將成為不可或缺的主流散熱選項。

GS Factor Profile 
The Goldman Sachs Factor Profile provides investment context for a stock by comparing key attributes to the market (i.e. our universe of rated stocks) 
and its sector peers. The four key attributes depicted are: Growth, Financial Returns, Multiple (e.g. valuation) and Integrated (a composite of Growth, 
Financial Returns and Multiple). Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple are calculated by using normalized ranks for specific metrics for each stock. The 
normalized ranks for the metrics are then averaged and converted into percentiles for the relevant attribute. The precise calculation of each metric may 
vary depending on the fiscal year, industry and region, but the standard approach is as follows: 
Growth is based on a stock’s forward-looking sales growth, EBITDA growth and EPS growth (for financial stocks, only EPS and sales growth), with a 
higher percentile indicating a higher growth company. Financial Returns is based on a stock’s forward-looking ROE, ROCE and CROCI (for financial 
stocks, only ROE), with a higher percentile indicating a company with higher financial returns. Multiple is based on a stock’s forward-looking P/E, P/B, 
price/dividend (P/D), EV/EBITDA, EV/FCF and EV/Debt Adjusted Cash Flow (DACF) (for financial stocks, only P/E, P/B and P/D), with a higher percentile 
indicating a stock trading at a higher multiple. The Integrated percentile is calculated as the average of the Growth percentile, Financial Returns 
percentile and (100% - Multiple percentile). 
Financial Returns and Multiple use the Goldman Sachs analyst forecasts at the fiscal year-end at least three quarters in the future. Growth uses inputs 
for the fiscal year at least seven quarters in the future compared with the year at least three quarters in the future (on a per-share basis for all metrics). 
For a more detailed description of how we calculate the GS Factor Profile, please contact your GS representative.

In this note, we address the key FAQs from investors on Jentech after we initiated 
coverage on September 29 (link).
•
What is already priced into Jentech’s current share price? What is not yet 
factored-in which could drive further outperformance in its share price? 
Despite Jentech’s share price being up ~60% YTD vs Taiex’s 15%, we don’t 
sense that the market has priced in the opportunities of micro-channel lid to AI 
chips adoption soon. This is based on the majority feedback from our buy side 
customers, and their consensus is that micro-channel lid will be adopted in 
2H27 at the earliest. Second, micro-channel lid is a product that can replace the 
current cold plate module, but AVC (3017.TW), the biggest cold plate module 
maker’s share price is up ~80% YTD. We are more constructive vs. the Street 
on the adoption of micro-channel lid to start from 2H26 and become more 
mainstream in 2027 (details in below paragraphs), while Jentech will be the 
sole supplier in the first year of adoption and can still maintain its leadership 
in the upcoming years, given its solid technology leadership in the packaging-
level cooling solutions, especially for AI server chips. We believe any further 
confirmation in the upcoming months will be a major share price driver. On the 
other hand, we believe Jentech is one of the largest beneficiaries of the compute 
tray design upgrade in the next-gen AI server system, driven by the additional 
chips placed in the tray (for inference processing), as each incremental chip 
will require a lid as well, in addition to the existing AI GPUs and CPUs.
•
Why do we think micro-channel lid can be adopted in 2H26 vs consensus 
of 2H27? First, we believe the chip customer has been facilitating the related 
supply chain to test the micro-channel lid solution in order to realize faster and 
more meaningful spec upgrades. Based on our industry check, the current 
testing/qualification of micro-channel lid adoption at chip level has been 
smooth so far. Second, even if there are lingering supply chain issues before the 
production schedule of the next-gen AI GPU (expected in 3Q26), we believe 
the the customer will still adopt micro-channel lid “during the next AI 
GPU cycle in 2027” as soon as the supply chain issues are resolved (even 
after a few months of mass production already). This is also why we model 
~1mn units of micro-channel lid shipment in 2026, which is relatively 
conservative vs the total expected volume of 2.5-3mn units for next-gen AI 
GPU in 2026. Some investors may pushback stating that customers are likely 
to switch designs back to the existing solution if there are still issues before 
their MP schedule (e.g. the change of board design just a few months before MP 
of this GPU customer’s AI server system), which may cause delay in micro-
channel adoption. However, we believe the AI GPU customer holds a much 
higher conviction to adopt micro-channel lid this time, as the adoption will 
directly impact the “chip-level” performance of its AI GPU (vs. board-
level/system-level design changes previously), hence we maintain a more 
positive view on the micro-channel adoption schedule vs. the Street’s current 
expectations.

•
Why would the AI GPU customer pull-in its schedule of micro-channel lid adoption 
to 2H26, if cold plate can still solve the heat of its next-gen chip? In our view, the 
breakthrough of cooling component could increase the TDP (Thermal Design Power) / 
the performance of AI server chips significantly. We sense that it is positive for the value 
chain players in the accelerating spec competition race (as most of the peers are trying to 
have meaningful spec migration in their next-gen chips). Hence, although we understand 
that the cold plate enhancement could meet the chip TDP of more than 2000W for the AI 
chips in 2026, we believe this magnitude of upgrade is not meaningful enough for the 
leading AI chip customer. We believe AI GPU would adopt micro-channel lid as soon as 
possible once this new solution is ready for mass production scale, as this cooling 
component evolution could fulfill customers’ request to reach 5000+W in the foreseeable 
future. This upgrade could assure the leading AI chip customer to widen its spec gap vs 
peers.  
•
Implications. We keep our estimates largely unchanged in this note, with our 
2025E/26E/27E EPS at NT$37/NT$60/NT$135. Our Dec-26 PT remains at NT$3,650, 
based on an unchanged 27x 2027E P/E, in line with the company’s 5-year average P/E.

AirTAC reported September revenue of RMB591mn (+1% MoM, +24% YoY) / 
NT$2,592mn (+1% MoM, +22% YoY), leading 3Q23 revenue at NT$7,564mn (-5% 
QoQ, +24% YoY), which was roughly in-line with GSe/BBG consensus of 
NT$7,495mn/NT$7,538mn. We saw linear guide revenue continue to grow MoM 
from July to September and make the overall linear guide revenue to reach 
~RMB130mn, which is much higher than the 2Q linear guide revenue of 
~RMB90mn. Moreover, pneumatic market demand performance was also solid 
while we started to see better industrial customers’ conﬁdence on bottoming macro 
economics, leading to better investment demand in pneumatics. In September, 
energy lighting continued to be the strongest segment in terms of YoY growth 
(+100% YoY), followed by packaging / general machinery/ electronics (+25% YoY), 
and machine tool (+15% YoY) while textile revenue remains ﬂat YoY in September. 
However, both battery (-5% YoY) and automotive (-8% YoY) revenue declined YoY in 
September. 
For October, we expect monthly revenue to go down by 10% MoM to RMB533mn 
(-10% MoM, +20% YoY) / NT$2,338mn (-10% MoM, +18% YoY) due to the 20% less 
working days (vs. September). However, we expect both pneumatic and linear 
guide’s daily revenue will grow MoM. For pneumatics, which the company will not 
get constrained by inventories issues, will continue to recover on its daily revenue 
due to the bottoming demand environment in both infrastructure market (see here) 
and property market (here) supported by government’s stimulus/loosening policy. For 
linear guide, customer expansion and ramp-up of production should help the 
company to grow, despite the ongoing difﬁcult demand condition in machine tools 
customers. 
Overall, we continue to see AirTAC’s outperformance in the China FA market, which 
was mainly driven by the company’s leading market share position and business 
model (low production cost and more proactive pricing strategy) enabling the 
company to gain further market share during the market demand downcycle (see 
more details here). Moreover, we believe the China pneumatic market inventory 
condition is much healthier than other FA market due to the short lead time (1-2 
weeks at most during the upcycle) and different business model (prefer to have 
more direct sales), suggesting a much more favorable market supply demand 
outlook compared to key FA product segments. This enables pneumatic players to

GS Factor Proﬁle 
The Goldman Sachs Factor Proﬁle provides investment context for a stock by comparing key attributes to the market (i.e. our coverage universe) and its 
sector peers. The four key attributes depicted are: Growth, Financial Returns, Multiple (e.g. valuation) and Integrated (a composite of Growth, Financial 
Returns and Multiple). Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple are calculated by using normalized ranks for speciﬁc metrics for each stock. The 
normalized ranks for the metrics are then averaged and converted into percentiles for the relevant attribute. The precise calculation of each metric may 
vary depending on the ﬁscal year, industry and region, but the standard approach is as follows: 
Growth is based on a stock’s forward-looking sales growth, EBITDA growth and EPS growth (for ﬁnancial stocks, only EPS and sales growth), with a 
higher percentile indicating a higher growth company. Financial Returns is based on a stock’s forward-looking ROE, ROCE and CROCI (for ﬁnancial 
stocks, only ROE), with a higher percentile indicating a company with higher ﬁnancial returns. Multiple is based on a stock’s forward-looking P/E, P/B, 
price/dividend (P/D), EV/EBITDA, EV/FCF and EV/Debt Adjusted Cash Flow (DACF) (for ﬁnancial stocks, only P/E, P/B and P/D), with a higher percentile 
indicating a stock trading at a higher multiple. The Integrated percentile is calculated as the average of the Growth percentile, Financial Returns 
percentile and (100% - Multiple percentile). 
Financial Returns and Multiple use the Goldman Sachs analyst forecasts at the ﬁscal year-end at least three quarters in the future. Growth uses inputs 
for the ﬁscal year at least seven quarters in the future compared with the year at least three quarters in the future (on a per-share basis for all metrics). 
For a more detailed description of how we calculate the GS Factor Proﬁle, please contact your GS representative.  
M&A Rank 
Across our global coverage, we examine stocks using an M&A framework, considering both qualitative factors and quantitative factors (which may vary 
across sectors and regions) to incorporate the potential that certain companies could be acquired. We then assign a M&A rank as a means of scoring 
companies under our rated coverage from 1 to 3, with 1 representing high (30%-50%) probability of the company becoming an acquisition target, 2 
representing medium (15%-30%) probability and 3 representing low (0%-15%) probability. For companies ranked 1 or 2, in line with our standard 
departmental guidelines we incorporate an M&A component into our target price. M&A rank of 3 is considered immaterial and therefore does not 
factor into our price target, and may or may not be discussed in research.

 Positive implications for Bizlink from Credo's strong FY2Q26 
results, upbeat FY3Q26/FY26 guidance,  and comments on its

FY2Q26 (ended October 2025) results:
• Credo (CRDO.US, not covered) reported  revenue of US$268mn (+20% QoQ/
+272% YoY), exceeding the high-end of its guidance at US$230-240mn.
• Non-GAAP GM was 67.7% (+0.1ppt QoQ; guidance 64-66%) and net profit
was US$128mn (+30% QoQ/+943% YoY).
• Four  customers each contributed more than 10% of its revenue in FY2Q26,
i.e., 42%, 24%, 16%, and 11%, respectively.
FY3Q26 and FY26 outlook:
• Credo guided FY3Q26  revenue to be US$335-345mn (+27% QoQ/+152% YoY
at the mid-point, above consensus at US$248mn),  non-GAAP GM at 64-66%
(vs. consensus at 64.9%) and opex at US$68-72mn, leading to revenue
growth of more than 170%, non-GAAP opex growth  of more than 50%, and
non-GAAP NPM at ~45% for FY26.
• Management expects to see four hyperscaler customers above the 10%
revenue contribution threshold in FY26, with a fifth starting to contribute
initial revenues in FY2Q26 and  a skew toward FY2H26.
• It said it is on track for PCIE AEC design wins in FY26 and meaningful
production revenue in FY27.
• On top of strong growth from AECs (Active Electrical Cables), Credo sees
ALCs (Active LED Cables) being one of the next growth drivers in the coming
years. It targets  first product sampling in FY27 and initial revenue ramp in
FY28. It expects TAM for ALC to be at least twice as large as that for AEC, as
the former can deliver the same reliability and power profile up to 30 meters
of transmission distance.
Read-across:
• We see positive implications for Bizlink from Credo's continuous ramp of
AEC in scale-out networks now, and scale-up networks in the near future, as
well as ALCs in the longer term,
• We stay constructive on Bizlink as we think it will continue to benefit from
volume and dollar content growth from data/power interconnects, as well as
the transition into the subsystem assembly for the semi cap equipment
business (see our report).

What’s new: Tong Yang released its 9M23 operating data on 11 October, 
having released its 9M23 revenue data on 4 October (see our memo). We 
believe the increasing adoption of after-market (AM) components in the US 
is likely to make it a structural trend, which we see as a mid-to-long-term 
revenue driver. However, in the near term, we believe the upward EPS 
revision trend will be the share-price catalyst. We reaffirm our Buy (1) call. 
What’s the impact: Record-high quarterly EPS in 3Q23, mainly thanks 
to revenue, gross margin and operating margin beat. Tong Yang’s 
3Q23 revenue of TWD6,154m (+10.9% QoQ and +11.3% YoY) was ahead 
of our forecast and the consensus estimate by 6.1% and 4.8%, 
respectively, mainly due to the solid AM revenue and recovery in China 
OEM revenue. Its operating margin came in at 16.5% in 3Q23, ahead of 
our (14.9%) and the consensus (14.7%) forecasts. Its operating profit of 
TWD1,018m (+27.8% QoQ and +82.4% YoY) beat both our and the 
consensus forecasts by 17.6%, which we attribute to the upbeat gross 
margin from the AM business with improving operating leverage. With an 
FX gain of TWD187.4m, Tong Yang’s pre-tax profit of TWD1,238m (+30.4% 
QoQ and +43.4% YoY) beat our and the consensus estimates by 16.9% 
and 23.3%, respectively. Its gross margin was c.30% in 3Q23 (vs. our 
forecast of 28.9% and the consensus forecast of 28.8%), up from 29.0% in 
2Q23 and 24.6% in 3Q22. 
Solid order outlook for AM segment plus recovery of China OEM 
segment. Tong Yang’s AM order demand remains solid, especially from the 
US, Europe and Central and South America, thanks to the upcoming peak 
season and the promotion from State Farm AM adoption, which should be 
the key earnings driver for Tong Yang. Its OEM revenue improved MoM in 
September 2023 and we expect the momentum to carry forward into 4Q23, 
with an improving gross margin. We revise up our 2023-25E EPS by 6-7%, 
mainly after factoring in our more aggressive revenue and margin 
assumptions. 
What we recommend: We reaffirm our Buy (1) call and raise our 12-month 
TP to TWD100 (from TWD91), still based on a target PER of 18x applied to 
our 1-year forward EPS, backed by an accelerating earnings momentum 
over 2023-25E and a likely structural trend that will lift the AM penetration 
rate in the US. Our target PER is around the average of the stock’s past-3-
year range of 7-31x. Key downside risks: weaker-than-expected gross-
margin expansion and AM revenue. 
How we differ: Our 2023-25E EPS are 4-10% above the consensus, likely 
as we are more aggressive on its revenue and gross margin expansion.
